summary:
Tekirdağ province records no province-specific statute, enforcement action, incident or institution concerning transgender visitors. What a trans visitor to Tekirdağ stands under is the national framework of Turkey, carried on the parent record.

Under that framework, homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, subject to sex reassignment surgery, medical examination and court permission. There is no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Openly LGBTQ people are barred from serving in the Turkish military: a health regulation defines homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', conscripts who declare it must provide photographic proof, and the resulting 'unfit report' can leak and fuel later discrimination in public life. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised. When the 12th judicial reform package passed in 2026 the anti-LGBTQ provisions were removed from the bill, leaving only symbolic same-sex weddings possible.

Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years, with police using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants who defied the bans. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the LGBTI and Trans pride marches in Istanbul, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained. Three activists were remanded in prison on 29 June 2025 under Law No. 2911 and released on 8 August pending trial, while prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. Law No. 2911 governs the assembly bans and prosecutions recorded here, and it binds authorities in Tekirdağ as it does across Turkey.

In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values' that could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities.

Early-2026 press reports recorded that the government considered legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex'. Turkey placed 47th of 49 countries in ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking.
tangentialFactors:
The 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking places Turkey 47th of 49 countries, a comparative position rather than a rule a visitor will be shown at a checkpoint.

Press reports of considered legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' were unconfirmed as enacted law in the sources; whether such a provision has since passed is unresolved.

Openly LGBTQ people are barred from military service; the 'unfit report' issued on discharge can leak and fuel later discrimination in public life.

Same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised. The removal of anti-LGBTQ provisions from the 12th judicial reform package in 2026 left only symbolic same-sex weddings possible.

The December 2025 dissolution order against the Young LGBTI+ Association binds a Turkish civil-society organisation and constrains LGBTI+ organising generally.

There is no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the legislation reportedly considered in early 2026, criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex', has been enacted remains unresolved in the sources.

No Tekirdağ-specific enforcement data, incidents or local institutions were identified in the inventory; the province-specific layer is otherwise not sourced.
